title: Implement Power Function
description:
Implement pow(A, B) % C.
Given A, B, C, find (A^B) % C.

Note: the remainder must be NON-NEGATIVE.

Problem Constraints
-10^9 ≤ A ≤ 10^9
0 ≤ B ≤ 10^9
1 ≤ C ≤ 10^9

Example
A=2, B=3, C=3 → 8 % 3 = 2.
A=3, B=3, C=1 → 27 % 1 = 0.
story: Halve the exponent each call (binary exponentiation). Multiply by A only on odd exponents. Take %C after every multiplication. Finally fix sign with ((x%C)+C)%C.
plain: Pure recursion at B is O(B) — TLE for B = 1e9. Halve B each time → O(log B). All intermediate products use long and are taken mod C. Because A can be negative, the final answer is normalised to [0, C) with ((res % C) + C) % C.
tale: You can't lift a 2^30 dumbbell directly. Instead lift the 2^15 version, square it, and you have your answer in 15 squares instead of a billion multiplications.
pitfalls: A can be negative, so the answer may come out negative — normalise with `((res % C) + C) % C` before returning.
`half * half` and `squared * A` can overflow int, so keep everything in long before taking `% C`.
Don't forget the base case returns `1 % C`, not `1` — when C is 1 the answer must be 0.

solutions.label: Brute — Loop Multiply
solutions.plain: Multiply A B-times, taking %C each step.
solutions.tale: One multiplication per beat. 1e9 beats = TLE.
approach: Loop B times: result = (result * A) % C.
solutions.pseudocode: r = 1; loop B times: r = (r*A)%C; return ((r%C)+C)%C
solutions.story: Educational only. Fails for B beyond ~1e7.

solutions.label: Optimal — Fast Power (recursive halving)
solutions.plain: pow(A,B) = pow(A, B/2)^2, multiplied by A if B is odd. Take %C after each multiplication.
approach: If B is odd → result = (sq * A) % C else result = sq.
Final: ((result % C) + C) % C for non-negative.
solutions.pseudocode: pow(A,B,C): if B==0 return 1%C; half=pow(A,B/2,C); sq=half*half%C; res = B odd ? sq*A%C : sq; return ((res%C)+C)%C
solutions.story: Optimal. O(log B), the textbook binary exponentiation pattern.

data.footer: Fast power: pow(2, 3) mod 3 via halving.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Why halving? 2^B requires log₂(B) squarings — turns O(1e9) into O(30).

script.label: Non-negative fix
script.overlay: Why the +C? If A were negative, intermediate products could be negative; this fix forces the answer into [0, C).

title: Greatest Common Divisor
description:
Given 2 non-negative integers A and B, find gcd(A, B).
GCD is the greatest integer that divides both A and B.
Note: gcd(0, 0) = 0.

Problem Constraints
0 ≤ A, B ≤ 10^9

Example
A=6, B=9 → 3. A=6, B=12 → 6.
story: Euclidean: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a%b), with gcd(a, 0) = a. O(log min(a,b)).
plain: Brute is loop from min(A,B) down to 1 — O(min). Euclidean halves at every step in the worst case (Fibonacci pair) → O(log min). Two lines: if (B == 0) return A; else return gcd(B, A % B).
tale: Two ropes of length A and B; subtract the shorter from the longer until they match. Modular replaces the subtractions with one division step.
pitfalls: Watch the base case: when B is 0 you return A, and that also handles gcd(0, 0) = 0 for free.
Order matters only on the first call — `gcd(A, B)` with A smaller just swaps them once, don't add a special swap.
Inputs can be 0, so don't assume A % B is always safe — the recursion stops before B ever hits 0 as a divisor.

solutions.label: Brute — Linear Scan
solutions.plain: Try every divisor from min(A,B) downward until both modulus 0.
solutions.tale: Knock on every door until both open.
approach: Edge: if A == 0 → return B; if B == 0 → return A.
For d = min(A,B) down to 1: if A%d == 0 && B%d == 0 → return d.
solutions.pseudocode: for d in min(A,B)..1: if A%d==0 and B%d==0: return d

solutions.label: Optimal — Euclidean Recursion
solutions.plain: Replace (A, B) with (B, A % B) until B becomes 0.
solutions.tale: Each call shrinks the bigger number to a remainder; log steps until zero.
solutions.pseudocode: gcd(A, B) = A if B==0 else gcd(B, A%B)
solutions.story: Optimal. Iterative version trivially in a while-loop.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Key identity: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b).

script.label: gcd(6, 9) → gcd(9, 6%9=6)
script.msg: First call swaps so the smaller goes second next time.

script.label: gcd(3, 0) = 3
script.overlay: Why log? Each step shrinks B by at least a factor of φ (Fibonacci bound). 1e9 → ~45 steps.

title: Pair Sum divisible by M
description:
Given an array A of N integers and integer B, count the number of pairs (i, j) with i < j such that (A[i] + A[j]) % B == 0.
Return the count mod 10^9 + 7.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5
1 ≤ A[i], B ≤ 10^9

Example
A = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], B = 2 → 4 pairs: (1,3)(1,5)(3,5)(2,4).
story: Group elements by remainder r = A[i] % B. Pairs with sum divisible by B: r and (B−r) must complement, plus the buckets r=0 and r=B/2 (if B even) pair within themselves.
plain: Brute O(N²) loops every pair. Optimal builds freq[r] = number of A[i] with A[i]%B == r, then: result = C(freq[0],2) + Σ_{r=1..B/2-1} freq[r]*freq[B-r] + (B even ? C(freq[B/2],2) : 0). Returns mod 1e9+7.
tale: Sort socks by colour first. Pairs of identical colour 0 (mod B), pairs of complementary colours (r and B−r), and pairs of the self-complement colour B/2.
pitfalls: `freq[r] * freq[B-r]` can overflow int with N up to 1e5, so cast to long before multiplying.
The middle stops at `r < B - r`, so handle r=0 and r=B/2 (only when B is even) separately as self-pairs with n*(n-1)/2.
`new int[B]` blows up when B is near 1e9 — this array version only works for small B, use a HashMap otherwise.

solutions.label: Brute — All Pairs
solutions.tale: Try every couple at the party.
approach: ans = 0; loop i = 0..N-1; loop j = i+1..N-1.
solutions.pseudocode: for i; for j>i: if (A[i]+A[j])%B==0: ans++

solutions.label: Optimal — Remainder Frequency Map
solutions.plain: Bucket by A[i]%B, then count complementary bucket pairs.
solutions.tale: Sort by colour, then read off pair counts in one sweep.
approach: Build freq array of size B: freq[A[i] % B]++.
For r = 1 while r < B - r: ans += freq[r] * freq[B - r].
Take mod 1e9 + 7 at each step (use long).
solutions.pseudocode: freq[A[i]%B]++; ans=C(freq[0],2)+Σ freq[r]*freq[B-r] for r in 1..B/2-1 + (B%2==0 ? C(freq[B/2],2) : 0)
solutions.story: Optimal. O(N+B) — and since B can be up to 1e9 you may want a HashMap variant when B is large.

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: A=[1,2,3,4,5], B=2. Build freq of remainders.
script.overlay: Why remainders? (a+b)%B==0 ⇔ a%B and b%B are complementary mod B.

script.label: Self-complement r=B/2=1
script.overlay: Note: B is even ⇒ the bucket r=B/2 pairs with itself, use n*(n-1)/2.

title: Largest Coprime Divisor
description:
Given two positive numbers A and B, find the maximum X such that:
• X divides A (i.e. A % X == 0)
• X and B are co-prime (gcd(X, B) == 1).

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ A, B ≤ 10^9

Example
A=30, B=12 → 5. A=5, B=10 → 1.
story: Repeatedly strip from A every prime factor it shares with B. After stripping, what remains is the largest divisor of A coprime with B.
plain: Brute: for every divisor d of A, check gcd(d, B) == 1, track max. Optimal: while gcd(A, B) > 1, divide A by that gcd; what remains is the answer. Each iteration removes at least one shared prime → O(log A) iterations × O(log) for gcd.
tale: Peel off the layers of A that overlap with B until the remaining apple is purely 'not-B'.
pitfalls: The loop only ends when gcd hits 1 — if you forget to divide A by g each turn it spins forever.
Dividing A by gcd(A,B) strips ALL copies of a shared prime layer, so don't loop over primes one at a time.
Answer can be A itself (when A and B are already coprime), so start from A, not 1.

solutions.label: Brute — Divisor Enumeration
solutions.plain: Enumerate all divisors of A; for each, gcd test with B; track max.
solutions.tale: List every divisor; pick the largest non-shared one.
approach: For d = 1..√A: if A % d == 0 → check d and A/d, update best if coprime with B.
solutions.pseudocode: for d in 1..sqrt(A): if A%d==0: test d, test A/d
solutions.story: Educational. √(1e9) ≈ 31623 — acceptable here but Optimal is one-liner.

solutions.label: Optimal — Strip Shared Primes via GCD
solutions.plain: While gcd(A, B) > 1, A /= gcd(A, B). Return A.
solutions.tale: Each loop removes a shared prime factor of A in one shot.
solutions.story: Optimal. Each iteration strictly reduces A's set of prime factors shared with B.

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: A=30, B=12. Strip shared primes of A with B.
script.overlay: Why divide by gcd? The shared prime factor(s) are exactly gcd(A,B); removing them once peels off ALL the shared structure for that prime layer.

script.label: gcd(5, 12) = 1 → stop
script.msg: 5 has no factor in common with 12. Return 5.

title: Divisor Game
description:
Scooby has 3 integers A, B, C. A positive integer is special if it is divisible by BOTH B and C. Count the special integers ≤ A.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ A, B, C ≤ 10^9

Example
A=12, B=3, C=2 → 2 (the special integers are 6 and 12).
A=6, B=1, C=4 → 1 (only 4 ≤ 6 is divisible by both).
story: An integer is divisible by both B and C iff it's divisible by lcm(B, C). Count multiples of lcm in [1..A] = A / lcm.
plain: Brute walks 1..A and checks. Optimal computes L = lcm(B, C) = B * (C / gcd(B, C)) and returns A / L. Use long throughout to avoid overflow when B and C are near 1e9.
tale: Two clock ticks every B seconds and every C seconds coincide every lcm(B,C) seconds; count how many coincidences fit before A.
pitfalls: `B * C` overflows int near 1e9, so compute lcm as `B * (C / gcd)` and divide first, in long.
Compute gcd before lcm — dividing C by gcd first is what keeps the multiply from overflowing.
The answer is `A / lcm` using integer division, which correctly floors the count of multiples.

solutions.label: Brute — Walk 1..A
solutions.plain: For each integer up to A, check divisibility by B and C.
solutions.tale: Read every number out loud and tally.
approach: count = 0; for x = 1..A: if x%B == 0 && x%C == 0 → count++.
solutions.pseudocode: for x in 1..A: if x%B==0 and x%C==0: count++

solutions.label: Optimal — A / lcm(B, C)
solutions.plain: Special ⇔ divisible by lcm(B, C). Multiples of lcm in [1..A] is A / lcm.
solutions.tale: Count beats of the joint rhythm in the time window.
approach: lcm = B * (C / g)  (use long; divide first to dodge overflow).
solutions.story: Optimal. The whole problem is one identity (lcm).

data.footer: Multiples of 3 ≤ 12 that are ALSO multiples of 2 → multiples of lcm(3,2)=6.

script.label: SETUP
script.msg: B=3, C=2, A=12. Multiples of 3 are shown.
script.overlay: Key: divisible by B AND C ⇔ divisible by lcm(B,C).

script.label: Answer = A / lcm = 12 / 6 = 2
script.overlay: Overflow watch: B*C may overflow for B,C near 1e9 — divide first: B * (C / gcd).

title: Mod Sum
description:
Given an array A of N integers, calculate the sum of A[i] % A[j] for all valid (i, j) pairs (i ≠ j or i == j allowed per Scaler convention — total over ordered pairs).
Return the sum modulo 10^9 + 7.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5
1 ≤ A[i] ≤ 10^3

Example
A = [1, 2, 3] → sum of A[i] % A[j] over all (i, j) = 5.
story: Values are bounded (≤ 1000) so iterate over distinct values, not indices: freq[v] = count of v. For every (a, b) with a < b, add freq[a]*freq[b]*(a%b). a%b for a > b reduces to (a mod b); pairs (a, b) with a == b or a multiple of b contribute zero.
plain: Brute O(N²) sums A[i]%A[j] over every pair. Optimal builds freq[1..1000], iterates b = 1..1000 and a = 1..b-1, adding freq[a] * freq[b] * (a % b) (since a < b, a % b == a). Plus an outer loop handling a ≥ b cases via multiples. O(MAX²) where MAX = 1000 = 1e6 ops.
tale: Instead of asking every person, ask 'how many people have value v?' once, then compute the answer per bucket.
pitfalls: Loop over the value range 1..1000, not the array indices — N is huge but values are tiny.
`freq[a] * freq[b] * (a%b)` can overflow int, so cast to long and take `% MOD` between multiplies.
Pairs where a == b or a is a multiple of b contribute 0 — remember to add both directions (a<b and a>b).

solutions.label: Brute — All Pairs
solutions.plain: Double loop over array, sum A[i] % A[j].
approach: ans = 0; loop i, j over array; ans = (ans + A[i] % A[j]) % MOD.
solutions.pseudocode: for i; for j: ans += A[i]%A[j]

solutions.label: Optimal — Frequency over Value Range
solutions.plain: Build freq[1..MAX]. For every (a, b) with a < b add freq[a]*freq[b]*(a%b). When a ≥ b the contribution is 0 unless a > b; iterate over multiples for that case.
solutions.tale: Group by value, then enumerate cheap distinct pairs.
approach: For b = 1..MAX with freq[b] > 0: for a = 1..b-1 with freq[a] > 0 → ans += freq[a] * freq[b] * (a % b).
Take mod 1e9 + 7 each step; use long.
solutions.pseudocode: freq[v]++; for b: for a<b: ans += freq[a]*freq[b]*(a%b)
solutions.story: Optimal when MAX is small. For larger MAX, switch to harmonic-sum trick over multiples.

data.footer: Compute Σ A[i] % A[j] via freq-array.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Why value-range loop? Values ≤ 1000 → 1e6 inner ops, fixed; N can be 1e5 and the answer is unchanged.

script.label: Self pairs (a == b) → 0
script.msg: 1%1, 2%2, 3%3 all contribute 0. Plus pair (a>b) symmetric counted earlier.

script.label: Final adjustment for (a > b) reflective pairs
script.overlay: Mind: the actual solve uses a single loop over b and adds both directions inside it.

title: A, B and Modulo
description:
Given two integers A and B, find the largest integer M > 0 such that A % M == B % M.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ A, B ≤ 10^9, A ≠ B.

Example
A=5, B=10 → 5.
story: A%M == B%M ⇔ M divides (A−B). The largest such M is |A−B| itself.
plain: No loop needed. One identity: A%M == B%M iff M | (A−B). The largest divisor of any positive integer X is X itself, so the answer is |A − B|.
tale: Two clocks tick differently but show the same minute hand position; the largest such cycle equals the absolute difference of their times.
pitfalls: The whole answer is just `|A - B|` — no loop, since the largest divisor of A-B is A-B itself.
A - B can be negative, so take the absolute value; the problem guarantees A != B so it's never 0.
Don't overthink it — brute-forcing every M up to 1e9 will TLE.

solutions.label: Brute — Try every M
solutions.plain: Check every M from max down.
approach: For M = max(A, B) down to 1: if A%M == B%M → return M.
solutions.pseudocode: for M=max..1: if A%M==B%M: return M

solutions.label: Optimal — |A − B|
solutions.story: Optimal. Whole problem collapses to one expression.

script.label: Verify: 5%5 = 0, 10%5 = 0 ✓
script.msg: Both remainders match — 5 is the largest M.

title: Delete one
description:
Given an integer array A of size N, delete one element such that the GCD of the remaining array is maximum. Return the maximum GCD.

Problem Constraints
2 ≤ N ≤ 10^5
1 ≤ A[i] ≤ 10^9

Example
A = [12, 15, 18] → delete 15, gcd(12,18) = 6 → 6.
A = [5, 15, 30] → delete 5, gcd(15,30) = 15 → 15.
story: Build prefix[i] = gcd(A[0..i]) and suffix[i] = gcd(A[i..N-1]). The GCD of the array with A[i] removed is gcd(prefix[i-1], suffix[i+1]). Scan once.
plain: Brute is O(N²) — for each i, gcd of the other N−1 elements. Optimal precomputes prefix & suffix gcd arrays in O(N); each delete is then O(1) gcd combine. Edge cases: deleting i=0 gives suffix[1]; deleting i=N-1 gives prefix[N-2].
tale: Two cumulative arrays from each end; ask 'what if I cut element i?' → combine the running gcd from the left of i with the running gcd from the right.
pitfalls: Deleting the first or last element has no neighbour on one side — use suffix[1] for i=0 and prefix[N-2] for i=N-1.
gcd with 0 returns the other number, so seeding brute with g=0 is fine but never mix that into the prefix/suffix build.
You need both prefix AND suffix arrays — a single running gcd can't answer 'skip element i' in O(1).

solutions.label: Brute — Recompute Per Deletion
solutions.plain: For each i, gcd of every j ≠ i.
solutions.tale: Recompute the whole gcd each time.
approach: best = 0; loop i: g = 0; loop j != i: g = gcd(g, A[j]).
solutions.pseudocode: for i: g=0; for j!=i: g=gcd(g,A[j]); best=max(best,g)

solutions.label: Optimal — Prefix + Suffix GCD
solutions.plain: Precompute prefix and suffix gcds; each removal answers in O(1).
solutions.tale: Cumulative gcds from both ends; merge across the removed index.
approach: prefix[0] = A[0]; for i ≥ 1 → prefix[i] = gcd(prefix[i-1], A[i]).
suffix[N-1] = A[N-1]; for i ≤ N-2 → suffix[i] = gcd(suffix[i+1], A[i]).
For each i: g = i == 0 ? suffix[1] : i == N-1 ? prefix[N-2] : gcd(prefix[i-1], suffix[i+1]).
solutions.pseudocode: build prefix, suffix; for i: g = combine(prefix[i-1], suffix[i+1]); best = max
solutions.story: Optimal. Tail of the classic 'aggregate with one element removed' pattern.

data.footer: Delete one element to maximise gcd of the rest.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Trick: aggregate-with-one-removed → prefix + suffix arrays, O(1) per removal.

script.label: Delete i=1 → gcd(prefix[0], suffix[2]) = gcd(12, 18) = 6
script.overlay: Why this wins: 12 and 18 share factor 6; deleting the odd-one-out (15) frees up the larger common divisor.
